title: Name the Room Not the Movie
bigQuestion: How did films change the names people use for Chinese martial arts, and how can we find the real schools behind them?

story.title: A Poster and a Charter
story.kicker: A movie poster and a school charter use the same word in two very different ways.
paragraphs: Two pieces of paper hang in the front window of a small school near Chinatown in Chicago. One is an old movie poster. It shows a hero leaping over a temple roof, with red letters that promise ancient secrets. The word kung fu runs across the top in huge type.

The other paper is the school's charter, framed behind glass. It gives the name of the style the school teaches. It names the city in Guangdong where the style's teachers came from. It lists the school's teachers, one after another, for four generations. It gives the year the school opened.

A visitor notices that the two papers disagree. The poster uses kung fu to mean magic and mystery. The charter never uses the word at all. It names one style, one place and one line of real people, each with a name and a date.

Both papers tell a kind of history. The poster tells the history of films, studios and audiences. The charter tells the history of a school, a family of teachers and a community that moved across an ocean. A careful reader learns to tell them apart.
story.think: What can the charter tell you that the poster cannot? What can the poster tell you about its own time?

lessons.title: Spelling a Chinese Word
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese words are spelled in English letters by different systems, so one art can have several English spellings.
reading: Chinese is written in characters, not in an alphabet. To write Chinese words in English letters, people use a *romanization* system. In the 1800s, two British scholars, Thomas Wade and Herbert Giles, built one system. It is called Wade–Giles, and it gave English the spelling kung fu.

In 1958, the People's Republic of China adopted a new system called *pinyin*. In pinyin, the same word is spelled gongfu. Taiji replaced t'ai chi, and Beijing replaced Peking. In 1982, the International Organization for Standardization approved pinyin as a world standard.

Spelling also depends on the spoken language. Mandarin is the national language of China. Cantonese is spoken in Guangdong and Hong Kong. Many teachers who brought southern styles abroad spoke Cantonese. That is why English uses Cantonese forms such as Wing Chun and Hung Gar.

So one art may appear with several spellings on signs and in books. A reader who knows the systems can see that tai chi and taiji name the same art. Spelling changes do not make a new style. They show which language and which decade a writer came from.

words.d: a system for writing words from another script in English (Roman) letters
the romanization system adopted by the People's Republic of China in 1958
a Chinese language spoken in Guangdong and Hong Kong

look.title: Three Signs, One Art
look.text: Three signs hang in three cities. The first, from the 1970s, says T'ai Chi Ch'uan. The second, from the 2010s, says Taijiquan. The third, a park flyer, says simply Tai Chi. All three advertise classes in the same family style.
look.prompt: Which spelling system did each sign use? Why might the older sign use a different spelling?

check.q: Which romanization system gave English the spelling kung fu?
check.why: Wade–Giles, built by Thomas Wade and Herbert Giles, spells the word kung fu.

check.q: When did the People's Republic of China adopt pinyin?
check.why: China adopted pinyin in 1958; it became an international standard in 1982.

check.q: Why are Wing Chun and Hung Gar spelled in Cantonese forms?
choices: Their teachers abroad often spoke Cantonese
Pinyin has no letters for them
They were named by a film studio
check.why: Many southern teachers came from Cantonese-speaking Guangdong and Hong Kong.

lessons.title: Schools in Chinese America
lessons.mainIdea: United States immigration laws shaped when Chinese teachers could arrive, and schools grew inside Chinatown communities before opening widely.
reading: In 1882, Congress passed the *Chinese Exclusion Act*. It stopped Chinese laborers from coming to the United States. It was the first major U.S. law to shut out people of one nationality. Congress repealed it in 1943, during World War II, but kept a tiny yearly quota.

Chinese Americans built their own institutions under these limits. They formed family associations, merchant associations and benevolent societies. In Chicago, Chinatown grew around Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue from about 1912. The On Leong Merchants Association building there opened in the late 1920s. It is now the Pui Tak Center.

Martial arts often lived inside these community groups. Many lion dance teams trained with a martial arts teacher. They performed at Lunar New Year and at openings of businesses. Classes were often taught in Cantonese to members of the community.

The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended the old national quotas. Many more Chinese immigrants arrived, including teachers. At the same time, more schools began teaching students from outside Chinatown. By the 1970s, Chinese martial arts schools had opened in cities across the country.

words.d: an 1882 U.S. law that stopped Chinese laborers from immigrating; repealed in 1943
a community group that helps its members with needs such as jobs, housing and funerals
a U.S. law that ended the old national quotas and opened immigration more widely

look.title: An 1882 Law
look.text: The act suspended the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States for ten years. It also said that no state or federal court could admit Chinese people to citizenship.
look.cite: Chinese Exclusion Act, May 6, 1882 (47th U.S. Congress)
look.prompt: How might this law have affected the number of Chinese martial arts teachers in the United States before 1943?

check.q: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 do?
choices: It stopped Chinese laborers from immigrating
It made kung fu a school subject
check.why: The 1882 act shut out Chinese laborers and was not repealed until 1943.

check.q: Where did Chicago's Chinatown grow from about 1912?
choices: Around Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue
check.why: Chicago's Chinatown settled around Cermak and Wentworth from about 1912.

check.q: Which 1965 law ended the old national quotas?
check.why: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 opened immigration more widely.

lessons.title: Hong Kong Studios
lessons.mainIdea: Hong Kong film studios built martial arts films into a world genre, using story names that often differ from real school names.
reading: From the 1950s to the 1980s, Hong Kong was a center of Chinese-language filmmaking. The Shaw Brothers studio ran a huge studio lot there called Movietown. Golden Harvest, founded in 1970 by Raymond Chow and Leonard Ho, became its great rival. Both made hundreds of martial arts films.

Filmmakers worked in two main kinds of story. Each kind is a *genre*. The word *wuxia* means martial hero. Wuxia stories are usually set in the distant past and often include swords and flying heroes. Kung fu films, popular from the late 1960s, focused more on unarmed fighters in recent history.

Many films drew on wuxia novels. The writer Jin Yong, whose real name was Louis Cha (1924–2018), published famous wuxia novels in Hong Kong newspapers from 1955 to 1972. His stories include invented sects beside real places such as Shaolin and Wudang. Readers across the Chinese-speaking world knew his invented names.

In 2000, Ang Lee's film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon brought wuxia to world audiences. It was based on a novel by Wang Dulu. The film won four Academy Awards, including Best Foreign Language Film. Its sword schools and secret manuals come from fiction, not from school records.

words.d: a kind or category of story, film or art
martial hero; a Chinese genre of stories about heroes in the distant past
a company that makes films, often on its own large site

look.title: A Sect on the Page
look.text: A wuxia novel describes a mountain sect with a secret manual, a founder who lived three hundred years ago and a rival sect across a valley. The novel also mentions Shaolin Monastery, a real place in Henan.
look.prompt: Which details might be invented, and which one is real? How could you check?

check.q: What does wuxia mean?
check.why: Wuxia means martial hero, a genre of stories set in the distant past.

check.q: Which studio was founded in 1970 by Raymond Chow and Leonard Ho?
check.why: Golden Harvest was founded in 1970 and became Shaw Brothers' rival.

check.q: Where do the sword schools in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon come from?
choices: From fiction, based on a novel by Wang Dulu
check.why: The film adapts Wang Dulu's novel; its schools are fictional.

lessons.title: Bruce Lee's Short Career
lessons.mainIdea: Bruce Lee made four finished starring films in three years, and they made the word kung fu famous around the world.
reading: Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong. He acted in films as a child. In Hong Kong he studied Wing Chun with the teacher Ip Man. In 1959 he moved to the United States. He studied at the University of Washington and began teaching in Seattle.

In 1966 and 1967, Lee played Kato on the American television show The Green Hornet. Then he returned to Hong Kong and signed with Golden Harvest. The Big Boss came out in 1971. Fist of Fury and The Way of the Dragon followed in 1972. Each broke box office records in Hong Kong.

Enter the Dragon was made with the American studio Warner Bros. Lee died in Hong Kong on July 20, 1973, at age 32. The film opened in the United States weeks later. It became a worldwide hit and helped start a kung fu film *craze* in the West.

Lee's fame made the word kung fu known in many languages. His films named some real places and schools and invented others. His *legacy* includes films, a school name he created and his writings, later published by his family and students.

words.d: a sudden, widespread popular interest that often fades later
what a person leaves behind that others remember and use
the money a film earns from ticket sales

look.title: Bruce Lee's Starring Films
look.cite: Golden Harvest and Warner Bros. release records
look.prompt: How many years passed between Lee's first and last finished starring film?

check.q: Which teacher did Bruce Lee study Wing Chun with in Hong Kong?
check.why: Lee studied Wing Chun with Ip Man before moving to the United States in 1959.

check.q: Which film was made with Warner Bros. and released after Lee's death?
check.why: Enter the Dragon opened weeks after Lee died on July 20, 1973.

check.q: What role did Lee play on The Green Hornet in 1966 and 1967?
check.why: Lee played Kato on the American show before his Hong Kong films.

lessons.title: Wong Fei-hung on Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Wong Fei-hung was a real Cantonese healer and teacher who became the hero of more Chinese films than almost anyone.
reading: Wong Fei-hung lived from 1847 to 1925 in Guangdong province. He was a martial arts teacher linked with the Hung Gar style. He also ran a clinic that treated injuries with traditional Chinese medicine. His clinic was known as Po Chi Lam. Records of his daily life are few.

In 1949, a Hong Kong film called The True Story of Wong Fei-hung came out. The actor Kwan Tak-hing played Wong. Kwan went on to play him in dozens of films over the next decades. Few real people have appeared as heroes in so many films.

Later filmmakers kept the name but changed the stories. In Drunken Master (1978), Jackie Chan played a young, mischievous Wong. In Once Upon a Time in China (1991), Jet Li played Wong as a national hero facing foreign powers. Each film reflected its own decade.

A *screen persona* is the character audiences know from films. Wong's screen persona grew far larger than the records of his life. Historians separate the documented teacher and healer from the film hero. The Hung Gar schools that honor him keep their own lineage records.

words.d: the character that audiences know from films, which may differ from the real person
a southern Chinese style from Guangdong, linked with Wong Fei-hung
a long-standing Chinese system of healing that includes herbs and treatment of injuries

look.cite: Wong Fei-hung Memorial Hall, Foshan; Hong Kong Film Archive
look.prompt: How many years after Wong's death did the first film about him appear?

check.q: Besides teaching, what work did Wong Fei-hung do?
choices: He ran a clinic for injuries
check.why: Wong ran the Po Chi Lam clinic using traditional Chinese medicine.

check.q: Which actor played Wong in dozens of films starting in 1949?
check.why: Kwan Tak-hing first played Wong in The True Story of Wong Fei-hung, 1949.

check.q: What is a screen persona?
choices: The character audiences know from films
check.why: Wong's screen persona grew larger than the records of his real life.

lessons.title: Huo Yuanjia and Chen Zhen
lessons.mainIdea: Fist of Fury and Fearless use the real Huo Yuanjia and the real Jingwu Association, but their plots mix history with invention.
reading: Huo Yuanjia was a real fighter from Tianjin who died in 1910. He is linked with the founding of the Jingwu Athletic Association in Shanghai that year. Stories about his challenges to foreign fighters spread widely. Historians note that the details of those stories are hard to confirm.

Bruce Lee's 1972 film Fist of Fury is set at the Jingwu school in Shanghai just after Huo's death. Lee plays Chen Zhen, a student who seeks justice for his teacher. Chen Zhen is a *fictional* character, invented for the screen. Later films and television shows brought him back many times.

In 2006, Jet Li starred as Huo Yuanjia in a film called Fearless. It tells Huo's life as a story of pride, loss and change. The filmmakers invented or reshaped many events for drama. Fifteen years earlier, Jet Li had played Wong Fei-hung in Once Upon a Time in China.

A *historical film* is set in the past but is made to entertain. It may use real names, real places and real dates. It may also add invented people and events. Historians compare such films with records, the way they compare legends with steles.

words.d: invented for a story, not a real person or event
a film set in the past that uses real names and places but may add invented events
a real fighter from Tianjin, died 1910, linked with the founding of the Jingwu Association

look.title: Real or Invented?
look.text: A list of names from Fist of Fury: Huo Yuanjia, the teacher who has just died. The Jingwu school in Shanghai. Chen Zhen, the loyal student. The year, around 1910.
look.prompt: Sort the list into real and invented. Which item on the list is fictional, and how do you know?

check.q: Who is Chen Zhen?
choices: A fictional student invented for film
check.why: Chen Zhen was invented for Fist of Fury and returned in later films.

check.q: Where is Fist of Fury set?
check.why: The film takes place at the Jingwu school just after Huo's death in 1910.

check.q: What is true of a historical film?
choices: It must use only real events
It is always made by a government
It may add invented people to real settings
check.why: Historical films mix real names and places with invented events.

lessons.title: Ip Man: Teacher and Film Hero
lessons.mainIdea: Ip Man was a real Wing Chun teacher in Foshan and Hong Kong; films since 2008 turned his life into a patriotic drama.
reading: Ip Man was born in Foshan, Guangdong, in 1893. He learned Wing Chun there. In 1949, as the Chinese Civil War ended, he moved to Hong Kong. In the early 1950s he began teaching Wing Chun to paying students. He taught there until his death in 1972.

Ip Man's students opened schools in many countries. His most famous student was Bruce Lee. Other students, such as his sons Ip Chun and Ip Ching, also taught widely. Many Wing Chun schools today trace their *lineage* through Ip Man.

In 2008, the film Ip Man came out, starring Donnie Yen. It shows Ip in Foshan during the Japanese occupation of the late 1930s and 1940s. Its most famous scenes are invented for drama. Sequels followed in 2010, 2015 and 2019. Their success brought many new students to Wing Chun schools.

The films present Ip as a *patriotic* hero who defends China's honor. School records present him as a teacher who ran classes and trained students. Both images are now part of how people remember him. Historians keep the two apart.

words.d: a line of teachers and students traced back through the generations
showing love and loyalty to one's country
a southern Chinese style from Guangdong, taught in Hong Kong by Ip Man

look.title: A Wall of Photographs
look.text: A Wing Chun school has a row of framed photographs on its wall. The first shows Ip Man in Hong Kong in the 1960s. Next come his student, that student's student and finally the current teacher. A small movie poster of Ip Man (2008) hangs by the door.
look.prompt: Which items on the wall record the school's lineage, and which record film history?

check.q: In which city was Ip Man born in 1893?
check.why: Ip Man was born in Foshan, Guangdong, and learned Wing Chun there.

check.q: When did Ip Man move to Hong Kong?
check.why: He moved to Hong Kong in 1949 and began teaching in the early 1950s.

check.q: Who starred in the 2008 film Ip Man?
check.why: Donnie Yen played Ip Man in the 2008 film and its sequels.

lessons.title: Origin Stories in School Names
lessons.mainIdea: Many style names honor founders from a school's own tradition, and historians label the stories behind them as tradition or legend when records are missing.
reading: Many Chinese style names contain a person's name. Hung Gar means Hung family. Its tradition honors Hung Hei-gun, a figure said to have learned at a southern Shaolin temple. Historians have not found records that confirm his life or that temple's story.

Wing Chun has a famous *origin story*. It says a Buddhist nun named Ng Mui taught a young woman named Yim Wing-chun, and the style took her name. Wing Chun schools tell this story with pride. Historians label it a legend, because no records from the time confirm it.

Choy Li Fut was founded, by its own tradition, by Chan Heung of Guangdong in 1836. By that tradition, its name honors two of Chan Heung's teachers, Choy Fook and Li Yau-san, and Fut, the Cantonese word for the Buddha. Here, the school's tradition gives a date and a founder. Outside records about him are few.

A school's *tradition* is what it teaches about its own past. Traditions carry meaning, honor teachers and build belonging. Historians report them respectfully. They also say clearly which parts are confirmed by records.

words.d: a story a group tells about how it began
what a group teaches and passes on about its own customs and past

look.title: Three Labels for One Story
look.text: A museum label about Wing Chun reads: 'According to Wing Chun tradition, the nun Ng Mui taught Yim Wing-chun, who gave the style its name. Historians have not found records from the time that confirm this story. Records of Wing Chun teachers in Foshan in the 1800s do exist.'
look.prompt: Which sentence reports a tradition, which reports a gap in the records, and which reports a record?

check.q: What does Hung Gar mean?
check.why: Gar means family; the style honors Hung Hei-gun from its tradition.

check.q: Why do historians label the Ng Mui story a legend?
choices: No records from the time confirm it
check.why: Wing Chun schools tell the story, but no records from the time confirm it.

check.q: What does the name Choy Li Fut honor, by its own tradition?
choices: Two of Chan Heung's teachers and the Buddha
check.why: By the school's tradition, Choy and Li are two of Chan Heung's teachers, and Fut is the Cantonese word for the Buddha.

lessons.title: Kung Fu on American Television
lessons.mainIdea: The TV series Kung Fu (1972–1975) spread the word to American homes, and its casting reflected Hollywood's long habit of giving Asian roles to white actors.
reading: Kung Fu was an American television series on the ABC network from 1972 to 1975. It told of Kwai Chang Caine, a half-Chinese man trained at the Shaolin Monastery. Caine wanders the American West in the 1800s. Each episode mixed a Western with flashbacks to his temple training.

The role of Caine went to David Carradine, a white American actor. For decades, Hollywood had often given Asian roles to white actors. This practice is called *yellowface* when makeup or costume is used to make a white actor look Asian. Asian American actors and groups criticized the practice. They said it kept them out of roles and spread a *stereotype* of Asian people.

The show's temple scenes came from the writers' imagination. They mixed real names, such as Shaolin, with invented lessons and sayings. For many American viewers, the show was their first picture of Chinese martial arts. That picture was a film set, not a real monastery.

Fans of Chinese arts and scholars have since pointed out what the series got wrong. Later films and shows cast more Asian and Asian American actors in leading roles. The debate over Kung Fu is now part of the history of how Americans learned the word.

words.d: the practice of using makeup or costume so a white actor can play an Asian character
a fixed, oversimplified idea about a group of people
choosing which actors play which roles

check.q: What is yellowface?
choices: Makeup or costume used so a white actor can play an Asian character
check.why: Asian American actors criticized yellowface for keeping them out of roles.

check.why: Critics said the show spread stereotypes about Chinese people and arts.

lessons.title: Karate in the Title, Kung Fu on Screen
lessons.mainIdea: The 2010 remake of The Karate Kid moved the story to Beijing and showed kung fu while keeping a title about karate, an Okinawan and Japanese art.
reading: The first Karate Kid film came out in 1984. It is set in Southern California. The actor Pat Morita played Mr. Miyagi, a teacher from Okinawa. Karate grew on Okinawa, once the Ryukyu Kingdom. So the film's title and its teacher matched.

In 2010, a remake of The Karate Kid came out. It starred Jaden Smith and Jackie Chan. The story moved to Beijing, China. Jackie Chan plays a maintenance man named Mr. Han, who teaches Chinese martial arts. Yet the English title still said karate.

Reviewers pointed out the mismatch at the time. Karate and Chinese arts come from different places and have different histories. The studio kept the famous title because audiences already knew it. A *brand* is a well-known name used to sell a product.

This case shows how names can travel apart from the things they name. A film title can follow what sells tickets. A school name follows its style, its place and its teachers. Careful readers ask which kind of name they are reading.

words.d: a new film made from the story of an older film
a well-known name used to sell a product
an island group, once the Ryukyu Kingdom and now part of Japan, where karate grew

check.why: The remake moved the story to Beijing, China.

check.why: Karate grew on Okinawa; the 1984 film's Mr. Miyagi came from there.

check.q: Why did the studio keep the title The Karate Kid in 2010?

lessons.title: Jeet Kune Do: Naming a New Art
lessons.mainIdea: In 1967 Bruce Lee gave his own approach a new name, Jeet Kune Do, showing that martial art names can be created by one person at one date.
reading: Bruce Lee opened schools in Seattle, in Oakland in 1964 and in Los Angeles in 1967. He called the early schools the Jun Fan Gung Fu Institute. Jun Fan was his Chinese name. His teaching began from Wing Chun but drew on many other arts.

In 1967, Lee chose a new name: *Jeet Kune Do*. In Cantonese it means the way of the intercepting fist. Unlike most older style names, this one has a known inventor and a known date. Lee also said he did not want it treated as a fixed style.

After Lee died in 1973, his students kept teaching. They disagreed about what the name should cover. Some kept a small, close group. Others taught more widely and mixed in other arts. Lee's family later formed an organization to protect his name and legacy.

Jeet Kune Do is a clear example of a *founder* naming an art. It stands beside Hung Gar and Wing Chun, whose founders are known through tradition. It also stands beside film names like the invented sects in wuxia novels. Each kind of name has its own kind of evidence.

words.d: the name Bruce Lee gave his approach in 1967; Cantonese for the way of the intercepting fist
the person who starts a school, style or organization
